cards.explanation: The answer is 'I will not serve.' Israel broke the yoke, tore off the chains and said, 'I will not serve!' (Jeremiah 2:20). A yoke is the heavy wooden bar that ties an ox to its work, so they were snapping loose from their load. That's a big announcement to make out loud.

The answer is a rotten, wild vine. The LORD asks, 'How could you turn yourself before Me into a rotten, wild vine?' (Jeremiah 2:21). He planted a choice vine from the very best seed. Best seed, best start, and the vine still went rotten, friends. That's the sting in the question.

The word is stain. Even with lye and an abundance of soap, 'the stain of your guilt is still before Me' (Jeremiah 2:22). Lye is a harsh cleaner, so that's some serious scrubbing. And it still won't come out. No amount of elbow grease fixes that kind of mark.

The answer is False. Israel denies it. They say, 'I am not defiled; I have not run after the Baals' (Jeremiah 2:23). The LORD answers by pointing at their behavior in the valley and telling them to acknowledge what they have done. Hard to say 'not me' when the evidence is that loud.

The answer is False. The LORD says, 'All who seek her need not weary themselves; in mating season they will find her' (Jeremiah 2:24). No long search needed. The picture is a wild donkey at home in the wilderness, sniffing the wind, and those who seek her will find her.

The reason they give is that they love foreign gods. They say, 'It is hopeless! For I love foreign gods, and I must go after them' (Jeremiah 2:25). Notice they call it hopeless, but the reason is their own love for those gods. The LORD had just said they should keep their feet from going bare, and they said no thanks.

The word is father, friends. They say to a tree, 'You are my father,' and to a stone, 'You gave me birth' (Jeremiah 2:27). That includes their kings, officials, priests and prophets (Jeremiah 2:26). They said it to wood and stone, and the LORD says they turned their backs to Him and not their faces.

The LORD says to let the gods they made save them. He says, 'But where are the gods you made for yourselves? Let them rise up in your time of trouble and save you if they can' (Jeremiah 2:28). They'd made those gods themselves. So He challenges those gods to rise up and save Israel if they can.

The answer is True. The LORD asks, 'Why do you bring a case against Me? You have all rebelled against Me' (Jeremiah 2:29). Walking into court to argue with Him while the whole group has rebelled. That's a bold way to start a lawsuit.

The answer is that they accepted no discipline. The LORD says, 'I have struck your sons in vain; they accepted no discipline' (Jeremiah 2:30). In vain means it didn't get through. I think that's the saddest part, because the correction came and nobody took it in.

The answer is True. The LORD quotes His people: 'We are free to roam; we will come to You no more' (Jeremiah 2:31). He had just asked whether He'd been a wilderness to Israel or a land of dense darkness. Then He asks why His people would say that. A fair question.

The answer is days without number. 'My people have forgotten Me for days without number' (Jeremiah 2:32). A bride doesn't forget her wedding sash, and yet they'd forgotten Him for that long. That's a long, long stretch.

The answer is True, friends. The LORD says, 'you say, "I am innocent. Surely His anger will turn from me."' (Jeremiah 2:35). This comes after He mentions blood on their skirts and all these things. Then He says He will judge them because they say, 'I have not sinned.'

The word is judge. 'Behold, I will judge you, because you say, "I have not sinned."' (Jeremiah 2:35). The reason is right there in the verse. They claim they haven't sinned, and He says He will judge them.

The answer is that Egypt will disappoint them too. The LORD says, 'You will be disappointed by Egypt just as you were by Assyria' (Jeremiah 2:36). Assyria let them down, and the same is said of Egypt. Same disappointment, new address.

The answer is with their hands on their heads. 'You will leave that place with your hands on your head' (Jeremiah 2:37). The reason given is that the LORD has rejected those they trust, so they won't prosper by their help. I think hands on the head is the picture of someone with nothing left to hold on to.

The LORD asks whether they would return to Him. He says, 'you would return to Me?' (Jeremiah 3:1). He begins with a picture of a man who divorces his wife and she marries another, asking if he can ever return to her. Then He turns it on them, after saying they have played the harlot with many lovers. It's a heavy question, and it's the LORD asking it.

The reason is that Israel defiled the land. The LORD says, 'You have defiled the land with your prostitution and wickedness. Therefore the showers have been withheld, and no spring rains have fallen' (Jeremiah 3:2-3). The word therefore connects the two, friends. The reason is stated right there in the verse.

The word is ashamed. The LORD says, 'you have the brazen look of a prostitute; you refuse to be ashamed' (Jeremiah 3:3). Earlier He said a thief is ashamed when he is caught (Jeremiah 2:26). He sets that beside Israel, who refuses to be ashamed.

The answer is False. After their words about His anger, the LORD says, 'This you have spoken, but you keep doing all the evil you can' (Jeremiah 3:5). They talk like a child calling out to a father, and then they keep doing it. The words were there, but the turning wasn't.
